summary: PR #334's new PhysicsLabRuntime transition guard is bypassable because the returned Runtime facade still stores its mutable authority capabilities and guard state as caller-visible fields (`_registry`, `_fidelity`, `_entityIds`, `_disposed`, `_transitionInFlight`). A capture/transition callback can capture the runtime reference and mutate those fields/capabilities directly instead of reentering public step()/dispose(), allowing registry/fidelity population changes while the transition transaction flag is true. The runtime must keep authority capabilities and mutable transaction state closure-private (for example an opaque/frozen facade backed by private state) so callback code cannot bypass the public mutation fence.
evidence: PR #334 exact head 3475ca65f86e1dbb63e0d4d985ca5e4b3fd7c625 defines RuntimeImpl with caller-visible `_registry`, `_fidelity`, `_entityIds`, `_disposed`, and `_transitionInFlight` fields and returns that mutable table directly from PhysicsLabRuntime.new().

assertMutationAllowed() only protects public step()/dispose(); it does not mediate direct calls through the leaked registry/fidelity capabilities or direct writes to `_transitionInFlight`/`_disposed`.

A transition observer can capture the same runtime variable and call `(runtime :: any)._registry.unregister(otherEntityId)` while `_transitionInFlight` is true. The observer can then return normally, letting the outer entity transition continue while registry and FidelityManager populations have already diverged for the unrelated entity.

WorldEntity.createRegistry() intentionally keeps backing records closure-private and grants mutation only through the returned registry capability; storing that capability on the public runtime facade leaks exactly the authority the new transition fence is intended to mediate.
PR #334 adversarial tests exercise public dispose()/step() reentry but do not attempt direct facade/capability mutation from callbacks.
